content:
Summary Report: “FPT University Workshop – From Prototype to Production” Event Information Event: FPT University Workshop, organized by First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Theme: Secure, reliable and scalable enterprise AI on the cloud Format: Workshop with two main parts: moving AI from prototype to production, and case studies. Event Objectives Explain the gap between an academic AI prototype and an enterprise AI system Present the four pillars of production AI (security, scalability, reliability and cost) and how the cloud supports them Learn from real case studies: Cox Automotive, Mobileye and Duolingo Introduce Amazon Bedrock AgentCore as a foundation for running agents in an enterprise Speakers Khang Duong – FCAJ member Phuong Huyen – AI Engineer Fresher, FPT Software Nguyen Lam Anh – AI Engineer, FCAJ Key Highlights Session 1: From Prototype to Production – Secure, Reliable, Scalable Enterprise AI on the Cloud One restaurant, one story
The speaker used a restaurant analogy throughout the session:
Prototype = a home kitchen Enterprise AI = a restaurant chain Cloud = a central kitchen AI in the enterprise
The flow is Data (ingredients) → AI model (the chef) → Feature (the dish) → Users (customers) AI is usually a feature inside a product, for example recommendations, a support chatbot or fraud detection Academic AI vs. enterprise AI
Aspect Academic AI (home kitchen) Enterprise AI (restaurant chain) Goal Accuracy Business value Data Clean, fixed dataset Real, ever-changing data Users A few people Millions of users Operation One-off run 24/7, no downtime More than a model
The model is only “the recipe”. A production system also needs a data pipeline, security, scalability, reliability, monitoring and cost control Elastic scalability: a fixed kitchen wastes capacity when demand is low and fails when demand peaks, while an elastic kitchen follows demand. On AWS, Lambda automatically clones itself, Auto Scaling adds or removes capacity, and a Load Balancer shares the load Reliability: if one oven breaks, a backup is ready. Tools include health checks, retry, failover and alarms Cost efficiency: do not keep everything running when nobody is there. Use pay-per-use, right-sizing and caching The role of the cloud
Built-in security, scaling on demand, backup zones for reliability and pay-as-you-go pricing The shared responsibility is clear: AWS manages the infrastructure, and you manage your data and usage Session 2: From Prototype to Production – Case Study Cox Automotive
29,000+ employees on five continents, 2.3 billion online interactions a year (first-party data) and 57 agentic AI opportunities identified Business areas: car buying and selling, auctions, dealer software and fleet services Key question: “How do you build automated AI solutions that users will trust?” Approach: standardize the foundation first with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore AgentCore Runtime: one runtime for all agents, covering deployment, monitoring, error handling and security patterns; it runs Strands multi-agent systems AgentCore Identity: granular, role-based permissions for each agent Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: screens inputs and outputs, with multi-layered security and prompt hardening AgentCore Memory: context across sessions and customer preferences AgentCore Observability: logs every interaction so multi-step reasoning can be debugged Mobileye
Skilled engineers were spending their time answering status tickets: 66% of support tickets were routine status inquiries, and each ticket took about 15 clicks across several backend systems Context: 230M+ EyeQ chips deployed, with a data pipeline ingesting thousands of drive-recording sessions every day Why rule-based automation was not enough: scripts and decision trees handle predictable queries but not the variety of real requests Hybrid design where on-premises tickets meet a cloud agent: On-premises: a local orchestrator pulls tickets and posts replies; the ticket system is not reachable from AWS AWS AgentCore: the support agent runs on AgentCore Runtime, and credentials stay in Secrets Manager and are never exposed Mobileye services: a data pipeline MCP server provides live status, logs and errors, and an LLM gateway serves Claude with quota management AgentCore Observability traces each request through the MCP tool calls to the reply There is no inbound path into the on-premises network, and live data reaches the model at inference time through MCP Session 3: AI in Enterprise (Part 2) – Enterprise Challenges and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Today’s journey
Duolingo case study: why shared AI platforms matter Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Strands, Runtime and the AgentCore map Key Takeaways Production Mindset A prototype answers “does the model work?”, while production answers “does the system work for everyone, all the time, at a sustainable cost?” The model is one ingredient; the data pipeline, security, scaling, reliability, monitoring and cost matter just as much Cloud Architecture Elastic services (Lambda, Auto Scaling, Load Balancer) fit changing demand better than fixed capacity Reliability comes from health checks, retries, failover and alarms Pay-per-use, right-sizing and caching keep costs under control Enterprise Agents Standardizing the foundation first (runtime, identity, guardrails, memory, observability) lets many agents share the same safe base Hybrid designs can connect on-premises systems to cloud agents without opening inbound access MCP lets agents use live data at inference time Applying to Work Think beyond the model in my AI projects by planning the data pipeline, monitoring and cost from the start Design for changing data and many users instead of a single clean dataset Use serverless and auto scaling (Lambda, Auto Scaling, Load Balancer) for AI demos that may get unpredictable traffic Add reliability basics such as health checks, retries and alarms Try Amazon Bedrock AgentCore components (Runtime, Identity, Memory, Observability) for a small agent project Keep credentials in Secrets Manager and add guardrails to filter inputs and outputs Event Experience Attending the FPT University Workshop helped me see how AI moves from a classroom prototype to a system that real users depend on.
Learning from speakers The restaurant analogy made abstract cloud and AI ideas easy to remember and compare. Hearing from a fresher AI engineer at FPT Software made the path from study to real projects feel reachable. Real case studies Cox Automotive and Mobileye showed how large companies use AgentCore, guardrails and MCP to build agents that people can trust. The Mobileye case showed that automating routine work frees skilled engineers for harder problems. Networking and discussions I had the chance to exchange ideas with FCAJ members, students and engineers who work with AI on the cloud. Lessons learned Enterprise AI is judged by business value, reliability and trust, not accuracy alone. Standardizing a shared foundation makes it easier to scale many AI use cases safely. The cloud lets a small team handle infrastructure needs that once required a large operation. Some event photos Overall, the workshop gave me a clear picture of what it takes to turn an AI prototype into a secure, reliable and scalable product.

title: Blog 1
content:
AMAZON BEDROCK AGENTCORE: THE MISSING INFRASTRUCTURE FOR PRODUCTION AI AGENTS Getting an AI agent to work on your laptop is easy: a framework like LangGraph or Strands Agents, a model, and a few dozen lines of code. The hard part is what comes next: running it for thousands of users while keeping it secure, observable and under control. That is the problem Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is built to solve.
What is AgentCore? AgentCore is an AWS platform for building, deploying and operating agents at scale. It is made of modular services: use them together or pick only the ones you need.
It is also framework- and model-agnostic. It works with CrewAI, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, Google ADK, OpenAI Agents SDK and Strands Agents, and with models outside Amazon Bedrock. You keep your agent code, and AgentCore takes care of the infrastructure around it.
The main building blocks Service What it does Runtime Serverless hosting for agents and tools. Every user session is isolated, and you pay for the CPU and memory actually used. Memory Short-term (within a conversation) and long-term (across sessions) memory, without building your own storage layer. Gateway Turns APIs, Lambda functions and other services into tools the agent can call. Supports MCP. Identity Lets agents sign in to external systems (Slack, Salesforce, internal APIs) on behalf of a user. Works with Cognito, Entra ID and Okta. Code Interpreter / Browser Run code in a sandbox and interact with websites. Observability, Evaluations, Policy Traces in CloudWatch, quality evaluation, and rules for what the agent may do. The part I like most: Policy Agents act: they call APIs, issue refunds, change data. Telling the model in a prompt to “be careful” is fragile.
Policy moves that control out of the agent. Rules are written in Cedar and enforced at the Gateway. With a Policy Engine in ENFORCE mode, every tool call is checked before it runs, so safety no longer depends on the model behaving well.
When should you use it? Use it when you already have a working prototype and now need session isolation, access control and monitoring. For a small demo or a class project, a simple setup is probably enough. AgentCore is built for production scale, and all its services support VPC connectivity, which helps when data must stay private.
Hands-on: deploy your first agent This follows the official quickstart using the AgentCore CLI.
Prerequisites: an AWS account with credentials configured, Node.js 20.12+, Python 3.10+, and uv.
1. Install the CLI
npm install -g @aws/agentcore agentcore --version If this prints an error, an old Python agentcore command may be shadowing it. Run pip uninstall bedrock-agentcore-starter-toolkit and open a new terminal.
2. Create a project (a Python agent using Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock, plus an AgentCore Memory resource)
agentcore create --name MyProject --template agent-python-strands cd MyProject 3. Test locally. This opens a browser inspector where you can chat with the agent and view traces.
agentcore dev --mode browser 4. Deploy. The first deploy takes a few minutes because CDK bootstraps your account.
agentcore build agentcore deploy agentcore status 5. Invoke the deployed agent
agentcore invoke --runtime agent --payload '{"prompt":"Hello, what can you do?"}' 6. Check logs and traces
agentcore logs runtime --since 30m agentcore traces runtime list --since 30m 7. Clean up to avoid unexpected charges
agentcore remove all --yes agentcore deploy --yes From here, agentcore add memory, agentcore add gateway and agentcore add runtime let you attach more capabilities, followed by another agentcore deploy.
Key takeaways The bottleneck for AI agents is no longer the model; it is the infrastructure around it: memory, access, monitoring and control. Modular, framework-agnostic services let you move an existing agent to production without rewriting it. Enforce what an agent may do at the infrastructure layer (Policy), not only in the prompt. References What is Amazon Bedrock AgentCore? (AWS Docs) Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (AWS Prescriptive Guidance) Get started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (AWS Docs)

title: Event 3
content:
Summary Report: “FCAJ Meetup – First Cloud AI Journey” Event Information Time: 08:30, Saturday, October 24, 2026 Location: 26F – Bitexco Financial Tower Format: Meetup for networking and knowledge sharing, counted as one event; registration on the portal Event Objectives Share practical knowledge on securing web applications with AWS Security Agent Explain AI agent concepts and the architecture of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime and Memory) Introduce Kiro Crew, a persistent AI companion for developers Create a space for students and practitioners to exchange ideas Speakers Thinh Nguyen – DevSecOps/Cloud Engineer, Styl Solutions, First Cloud AI Journey Xuan An – Leader, AWS Student Builder Group HCMUTE Khoa Kieu – Technical Lead Nghi Danh – AWS Community Builder Key Highlights Session 1: Securing Your Web Apps With AWS Security Agent The security bottleneck
Time-consuming: manual pentests take weeks Expensive: high daily rates for specialized people Inconsistent: coverage depends on the pentester’s mood and skill High operational costs: third-party audits cost $5k–$20k per engagement Meet the Frontier Agent
Autonomous reasoning: powered by Amazon Bedrock, it plans and executes security tasks without human intervention Full lifecycle: covers design review, code security and active penetration testing Verifiable findings: unlike LLM chatbots, it verifies vulnerabilities by attempting real exploitation Three capabilities
Design Security Review: upload Markdown docs or Terraform code, verify against managed packs (PCI DSS, NIST CSF, AWS Well-Architected), and check whether the design meets security requirements. Free tier: 200 reviews/month Code Security Review: integrated into GitHub/GitLab pull requests, comments directly on lines of code, suggests valid patches through auto-PR fixes, and scans for vulnerabilities and secrets. Free tier: 1,000 PR reviews/month Automated Pentesting: an autonomous agent attacks the running application with multi-step exploit chains (for example IDOR → XSS), authenticates like a real user, and provides a detailed attack graph with verifiable proof Session 2: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Master Class on Runtime and Memory Architecture Agenda: AI agent / Agentic AI / Agentic system → overview of AgentCore → AgentCore Runtime → AgentCore Memory
AI agent vs. agentic AI vs. agentic system
AI agent: a software entity that performs a specific task autonomously within boundaries. Narrow scope, for example a ticket triage bot that classifies support requests and assigns priority Agentic AI: a broader approach that plans, reasons and coordinates actions toward a goal with limited supervision. For example, a research assistant that plans steps, searches sources, summarizes findings and revises its plan Agentic system: the actual software architecture that implements agentic AI using agents, tools, memory, orchestration and guardrails. For example, a customer support platform where one agent classifies tickets, another fetches account data, and the system routes, retries, logs and enforces policy Challenges in moving agents from prototype to production
Agent frameworks (Strands Agents, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI) make building easy, but production needs a lot of undifferentiated heavy lifting: Securely executing and scaling agent code Remembering past interactions and learning Identity and access control for agents and tools Agentic tool use for complex workflows Discovering and connecting custom tools and resources Understanding and auditing every interaction Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – an all-in-one platform to build, run and optimize agents at scale
Enhance with tools and memory: Memory, Gateway, Browser tool, Code interpreter Deploy securely at scale: Runtime, Identity Operational insights: Observability Works with open-source frameworks (CrewAI, Google ADK, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents SDK, Strands Agents) and protocols (HTTP, MCP, A2A, AG-UI) Ecosystem diagram: the app and models connect to Agent Runtime (any framework, agent instructions, local tools, context). The runtime works with AgentCore Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, Identity and Memory, and everything feeds AgentCore Observability.
Session 3: Kiro Crew – All in One Your Companion Keep work moving
Persistent, open-source dev workspace Remembers your context and learns how you work Lets you come back to progress, not a restart Three pillars
Persistent and self-improving: memory, lessons and skills carry across sessions Works while you’re away: cron, webhooks and heartbeat monitors 8 layers of defense with signed audit logs Control what your crew learns
Corrections become durable lessons Repeated workflows become named skills (the demo showed 70 skills) Plain Markdown: inspect, edit, scope and delete Same steering format as the IDE and CLI Knowledge graph with search
Stores decisions, preferences and project context Uses vector embeddings and full-text search Retrieves what is relevant, not everything Memory that survives restarts
Projects and context persist Long-running work checkpoints and resumes No re-prompting to get back to where you were Key Takeaways Security Mindset Manual pentesting is slow, costly and inconsistent; AI agents can automate it while keeping proof of every finding Security should cover design, code and the running application Agent Architecture Distinguish between an agent (one task), agentic AI (goal-driven coordination) and an agentic system (the full architecture) Production agents need runtime, identity, memory, tools and observability, not just a framework Managed platforms like AgentCore remove much of the repetitive infrastructure work Developer Productivity Memory and persistent context mean AI assistants do not start from zero each session Lessons and skills stored as plain Markdown stay transparent and controllable Autonomous work still needs guardrails and audit logs Applying to Work Use AWS Security Agent ideas to review design docs, Terraform and pull requests in my projects Practice the agent vocabulary and design my AI projects as agentic systems with clear tools, memory and guardrails Try Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime, Memory, Gateway) for a small agent prototype Experiment with Kiro Crew to keep project context and repeated workflows as reusable skills Record decisions and lessons in Markdown so they can be reused across projects Event Experience Attending the FCAJ Meetup at Bitexco Financial Tower was a useful, relaxed event focused on sharing knowledge among students and practitioners.
Learning from speakers The speakers explained complex topics with simple tables, diagrams and real examples. The agent concepts session helped me separate terms I often saw mixed together. Hands-on exposure Seeing the Security Agent workflow, the AgentCore ecosystem diagram and the Kiro Crew interface made the tools easier to imagine using. Networking and discussions I had the chance to exchange ideas with other students and community members from the AWS Student Builder and Community Builder groups. Lessons learned Production-ready AI agents depend as much on memory, identity and observability as on the model. Automation is most valuable when its results can be verified and audited. Giving users control over what an AI remembers builds trust. Some event photos Overall, the meetup gave me a clearer picture of how AI agents are secured, built and kept reliable in real projects.

title: Event 2
content:
Summary Report: “AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi” Event Objectives Show how enterprises can adopt agentic AI while keeping cost, data and processes under control Introduce Amazon Quick and Kiro as a unified AI platform for business and engineering teams Present AWS Security Agent for proactive application security from design to deployment Introduce MCP and the AWS MCP servers for connecting AI agents to AWS services Speakers Tuan Vo – Sr. Solutions Architect, G-AsiaPacific Vietnam (Session PRT201-S, Level 200) Trung Nguyen – Technical Account Manager, AWS Vietnam (Session DVT305, Level 300) Tan Huynh – Technical Account Manager, AWS Vietnam (Session DVT305, Level 300) Key Highlights Session 1: Adopt Agentic AI Without Losing Control The state of AI adoption in enterprises
Employees use AI every day, but leadership often does not know what tools are used, how, or where the data goes.
Business users: hard to tap internal data (CRM, customer records), poor automation (manual copy-paste), data governance risk, no audit trail IT / Engineering: no cost control (no visibility into token spend), no control over outside use (licenses used for personal purposes), cannot measure ROI, processes not standardized Conclusion: AI is being used, but not yet governed. Enterprises need one unified AI platform to control cost and data while improving productivity. Monitor — Control — Standardize
The core message of the session, applied to both business users and engineers.
Amazon Quick – Unified AI Agent Platform
One platform replacing multiple disconnected tools; available on desktop, web and mobile Enterprise intelligence: supports on-premises, cloud and SaaS data sources Automation: plans and executes complex workflows Security & governance: access control, guardrails, dashboard, audit Extending Quick (no-code to high-code): Custom Chat Agent, Quick Sight (BI and visualization), Research (in-depth analysis and exportable reports), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (custom multi-agent systems with security and governance) Kiro – Next-Generation IDE for Engineering
Available as IDE, CLI and ACP, covering Docs → Build → Package → Deploy → Operate Auto-select: Kiro picks the optimal model based on task complexity, which keeps cost down Models include Claude Opus 5 (complex reasoning, architecture), GPT 5.6 (general purpose, long context), Deepseek v3.2 (code generation, cost-effective), Minimax M2.5 (multilingual, fast inference), GLM 5 (reasoning) and Qwen3 Coder (code-optimized, low cost), plus 12 other models Governance & Process Standardization
Governance: usage dashboard, prompt logs, budget cap and alerts Process: AI-DLC, spec-driven development, property-based testing Goal: move from “using AI” to “governing AI” in software development Your Path Forward (3 phases)
Phase 1 – Assess (2–4 weeks): audit AI tools in use, find cost leaks, fragmentation and governance gaps, pilot Quick and Kiro with one team on a real use case Phase 2 – Migrate (1–3 months): roll out Quick to all business teams, onboard engineers to Kiro across the SDLC, centralize dashboards, budgets and audit logs Phase 3 – Extend (ongoing): standardize with spec-driven dev, hooks and AI-DLC, run usage analytics to optimize cost, build custom agents on Bedrock AgentCore Motto: Govern first — Migrate smart — Scale with confidence. Session 2: AWS Security Agent – Proactive AppSec from Design to Deployment Proactive security across the development lifecycle
Design review (minutes): evaluates documents against the security baseline requirements Threat model (minutes): analyzes application architecture and identifies security threats Code review (near real-time): source code security analysis on pull requests, diffs and full repositories Penetration testing (hours): discovers and chains validated vulnerabilities through tailored multi-step attack scenarios Works wherever applications are built and run: AWS, multicloud, SaaS and hybrid / on-premises What is AWS Security Agent? Context-aware autonomous penetration testing.
AI-powered pentesting: combines SAST, DAST, SCA and autonomous pentesting in one solution Context awareness: ingests design docs, APIs, IaC, threat models, user stories and endpoints to customize attacks Validated security risks: chains vulnerabilities into provable, reproducible attacks, reducing false positives and alert fatigue Summary of capabilities
Threat model is STRIDE-based and auto-generated from the codebase and design documents Fully managed by AWS, no infrastructure to set up Repository integrations: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Amazon S3 uploads Available in 9 supported regions Pricing: pay-as-you-go, $50 per agent-hour for penetration testing, metered per second, no upfront cost or minimum commitment Free trial: 2 months, 400 task-hours per month (included in the AWS Free Tier) MCP and AWS MCP servers
Agenda: ultrafast refresher on MCP and AWS MCP servers, Agent Toolkit for AWS, supercharging with your knowledge servers, Q&A AWS MCP servers: 9,700+ GitHub stars, 60+ servers, 300+ AWS services covered, 20+ community-authored articles Key Takeaways Governance Mindset AI adoption without visibility creates risks in cost, data and compliance Monitor — Control — Standardize is the guiding principle Start with an assessment and a small pilot before rolling out to the whole organization Technical Architecture One unified platform (Quick for business, Kiro for engineering) is better than many disconnected tools Auto-selecting models by task complexity balances quality and cost Security should be applied at every stage: design, threat modeling, code and testing MCP servers let AI agents work with AWS services in a standard way Modernization Strategy Phased roadmap: Assess → Migrate → Extend Measure ROI with usage dashboards, prompt logs and budget caps Standardize development with spec-driven development, AI-DLC and property-based testing Applying to Work Audit the AI tools used in my team and project and note the cost and data risks Try Kiro with spec-driven development in coursework and team projects Use Security Agent ideas (design review, threat modeling, code review) before deploying a project Experiment with AWS MCP servers to connect AI assistants to AWS resources Set budget limits and usage tracking when using AI or cloud services Event Experience Attending AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi gave me a practical view of how AI is adopted and secured in real organizations.
Learning from experienced speakers Speakers from G-AsiaPacific and AWS Vietnam shared real problems of enterprise AI adoption and concrete ways to solve them. The roadmap and pricing examples made the ideas easy to apply. Hands-on exposure to tools Saw how Amazon Quick, Kiro and AWS Security Agent fit into business, development and security workflows. Learned that governance (dashboards, logs, budgets) is as important as the AI model itself. Networking and discussions Questions during the sessions and conversations with other attendees showed how many teams face the same cost, data and security concerns. Lessons learned Control and standardization should come before scaling AI. Security works best when it starts at design time, not after deployment. Choosing the right model and tool for each task saves both cost and effort. Some event photos Overall, the event helped me see AI not only as a productivity tool but as a system that must be monitored, secured and governed.

Summary Report: “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” Event Information Time: Thursday, September 26, 2024, 09:00 – 12:00 Location: 26F, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Organizers: CMC Global in cooperation with AWS First Cloud Journey Format: In-person talkshow, combined with a Buildathon kickoff and a mock interview session Event Objectives Show that building an enterprise bot takes far more than calling an LLM API Explain the design mindset behind reliable bots: architecture, context handling, latency, cost and data protection Present how to deploy bots on AWS with Amazon Bedrock and serverless services Give participants practical career advice through mock interviews Speakers Bui Nhat Truong – Technical Leader, CMC Global Agenda Time Activity Details 09:00 – 09:30 Buildathon Kickoff Launch of the technical challenge series, explanation of the rules and evaluation criteria, and team networking 09:30 – 11:15 Talkshow: The Thinking Behind Building The Bot System design, data flow, RAG architecture and LLM orchestration on AWS 11:15 – 12:00 Mock Interview and Career Coaching Live mock interviews for Cloud/AI roles, feedback on answers and open Q&A Key Highlights Enterprise-grade bot mindset A bot for business use differs greatly from a chat window where someone types a prompt:
Context management: keep only the useful parts of the conversation history, which lowers token cost and avoids overflowing the context window RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): ground answers in the company’s own data through embedding models and a vector database Guardrails and safety: filter harmful input, defend against prompt injection and keep answers within company policy Deploying on AWS Amazon Bedrock and Knowledge Bases: access several foundation models through one standard API, with RAG built in Serverless compute: AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway handle event-driven webhooks and cost almost nothing while idle Credential security: store API keys and secrets in AWS Secrets Manager rather than hardcoding them in source code Quote from the speaker A great AI assistant is not decided by having the biggest model, but by sound architecture: how latency is controlled, how accurate the information is, and how well the system recovers from unexpected cases.
Mock interview session Interviewer’s view: Tech Leads and Solution Architects value problem-solving ability, honesty about what you know and the ability to learn on your own, more than memorized syntax STAR method: describe lab work and projects as Situation → Task → Action → Result Networking: a chance to talk directly with engineers from CMC Global and AWS Key Takeaways Design Mindset Treat a bot as a system to be engineered, not as a prompt wrapped around a model Plan for latency, cost, accuracy and failure from the start Technical Architecture Combine RAG, context control and guardrails to keep answers relevant and safe Use managed AWS services (Bedrock, Lambda, API Gateway, Secrets Manager) to keep deployment simple and cost-efficient Keep secrets out of repositories Career Mindset Show how you think, not only what you remember Use the STAR structure to present hands-on AWS projects clearly Applying to Work Design project chatbots with RAG and selective context management instead of sending the whole history to the model Add guardrails such as input filtering and prompt-injection checks to any bot I build Try Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for a small question-answering prototype Use Lambda and API Gateway for lightweight bot backends Move credentials to AWS Secrets Manager in my projects Practice STAR answers based on my AWS labs and course projects Event Experience Attending “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” gave me a practical view of what sits behind a bot that works reliably in a company.
Learning from the speaker The talk showed that model choice is only one part of the picture; architecture decisions matter just as much. Examples of context management and RAG made the ideas concrete. Technical exposure I saw how Bedrock, Lambda, API Gateway and Secrets Manager can fit together in one bot deployment. Mock interview and career guidance Watching live mock interviews showed what interviewers look for in fresher candidates. The STAR method gave me a clear way to talk about my own projects. Networking and discussions I had the chance to meet engineers from CMC Global and AWS mentors and ask about career paths in cloud computing and information security. Lessons learned A strong bot comes from disciplined design, not only a powerful model. Security habits, such as managing secrets properly, should be built in from the start. Clear, honest communication of how you solve problems matters in interviews. Some event photos Overall, the talkshow changed how I see chatbot projects: as engineered systems that must be fast, accurate, safe and affordable.

Create a gateway endpoint
content:
Open the Amazon VPC console In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint: You will see 6 existing VPC endpoints that support AWS Systems Manager (SSM). These endpoints were deployed automatically by the CloudFormation Templates for this workshop.
In the Create endpoint console: Specify name of the endpoint: s3-gwe In service category, choose AWS services In Services, type s3 in the search box and choose the service with type gateway For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. For Configure route tables, select the route table that is already associated with two subnets (note: this is not the main route table for the VPC, but a second route table created by CloudFormation). For Policy, leave the default option, Full Access, to allow full access to the service. You will deploy a VPC endpoint policy in a later lab module to demonstrate restricting access to S3 buckets based on policies. Do not add a tag to the VPC endpoint at this time. Click Create endpoint, then click x after receiving a successful creation message.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Prepare the environment
content:
To prepare for this part of the workshop you will need to:

title: Proposal
content:
Motorcycle E-Commerce & RAG Chatbot Platform A Serverless Motorcycle Parts Store and Intelligent Advisory Chatbot on AWS 1. Executive Summary This project addresses the challenge of advising on and retailing motorcycle parts online. The hardest part of this industry is the sheer number of part codes and motorcycle models, which makes it very easy for customers to buy the wrong part, while stores spend a lot of staff time answering chats. The system combines a Next.js e-commerce website with a RAG Chatbot (real-time part compatibility advice over WebSocket) on a 100% AWS Serverless platform. The solution automates consulting, processes orders asynchronously, provides strong security, and keeps operating costs extremely low.
2. Objectives & Scope Project Objectives
Consultation Automation: Build a real-time RAG AI virtual assistant to verify motorcycle spare parts compatibility across specific vehicle models and production years (response latency < 2s). Cost Optimization & Scalability: Leverage a 100% Serverless architecture on AWS, completely eliminating EC2 server maintenance overhead while maintaining operational costs below $6 USD/month. Asynchronous Business Processing: Apply Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) to decouple order checkout, inventory deduction, shipping fulfillment, and email notifications. Project Scope In-Scope: Next.js 14 SSR e-commerce web application and 5 backend Lambda microservices. Customer authentication and administrative Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) via Amazon Cognito JWT. RAG AI Chatbot cluster via WebSocket API Gateway (integrated with S3 Vector Store and Google Gemini 2.0 Flash) alongside an on-duty staff escalation mechanism (Human Handover). Integration with VNPay Sandbox online payment gateway and Giao Hàng Nhanh (GHN) Sandbox logistics fulfillment. Event-driven orchestration utilizing Amazon EventBridge, 3 SQS queues equipped with Dead Letter Queues (DLQ), and 3 background workers (Inventory, Shipping, Notification). Comprehensive Infrastructure as Code (IaC) automation via Terraform and GitHub Actions CI/CD pipelines. Out-of-Scope: Physical retail Point-of-Sale (POS) systems for offline brick-and-mortar stores and direct international credit card payment processing (Stripe/PayPal). 3. Problem Statement Current problems
Customers without technical knowledge often order the wrong components/parts (wrong motorcycle model, wrong spark plug size, wrong chain and sprockets, etc.), leading to a high return rate. Staff spend a lot of time repeatedly answering the same questions: does this part fit my bike, is it in stock, how much does it cost. Renting fixed servers (EC2/VPS) incurs monthly maintenance costs even though traffic is uneven between day and night. Solution
Build the online store with Next.js 14 SSR and 5 Lambda microservices (Catalog, Cart, Order, User, Payment) behind API Gateway. Integrate an AI RAG Chatbot through API Gateway WebSocket: it automatically searches for compatible parts in a vector store kept on S3 and answers customers immediately. For difficult cases or complaints, the bot automatically forwards the information (Human Requested) to staff by email. Apply an event-driven architecture (EDA): EventBridge and SQS decouple inventory deduction, shipping order creation, and confirmation emails, with a DLQ to prevent the system from clogging. Secure online payment through the VNPay gateway with HMAC-SHA512 digital signature verification. Benefits and return on investment (ROI)
Reduces by more than 60% the time staff spend on chat duty answering basic questions. Reduces the wrong-part purchase rate to below 5%, since the bot verifies the correct motorcycle model before the customer orders. Extremely low infrastructure cost thanks to the serverless architecture and the pay-as-you-go model. The expected payback period is 3–6 months. 4. Solution Architecture The whole system runs on a Serverless model with no physical servers to manage. Users access the website through the CloudFront CDN; APIs are called through API Gateway REST; real-time chat goes through WebSocket; background tasks are pushed into EventBridge and SQS.
AWS services used
Amazon CloudFront & Functions: CDN for delivering the website, injecting security headers, and acting as an Edge WAF that blocks XSS, SQLi, etc. AWS Lambda: 13 functions: Next.js SSR, 5 backend microservices (Catalog, Cart, Order, User, Payment), the RAG Chatbot cluster (Chat Authorizer, Chat Receiver, Chat Orchestrator, DynamoDB Sync To S3), and 3 background workers (Inventory, Shipping, Notification). Amazon API Gateway: Provides the REST API for the website and the WebSocket API for the real-time chatbot. Amazon DynamoDB: Stores 6 data tables (Products, Orders, Carts, Users, StorePolicies, ChatbotSessions); Streams are enabled to automatically sync data to the AI knowledge base, and PITR backup is enabled. Amazon S3: Stores static website files, product images, and the Chatbot’s vector knowledge files. Amazon EventBridge & SQS: Orchestrates order events and message queues, including a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ). Amazon Cognito: Manages registration, sign-in, and customer/admin authorization using JWT. Amazon CloudWatch & SNS: System monitoring and error alerts via email. Amazon CloudTrail: Audit trail of edits/changes. AWS Secrets Manager: Securely stores secret keys. Component design
Frontend: S3 (images, static files) and a Next.js SSR Lambda for fast loading, supporting part search and filtering by motorcycle brand (Honda, Yamaha, etc.). Backend Microservices: Handle adding to cart, placing orders, updating accounts, and the VNPay payment webhook. RAG Chatbot: Receives messages over WebSocket and matches vectors on S3 to generate accurate advisory answers. Event Workers: Lambda InventoryWorker (deducts stock), ShippingWorker (creates GHN shipping orders), NotificationWorker (sends Gmail to customers/staff). 5. Technical Implementation Implementation phases
Architecture design & Terraform: design the serverless architecture in draw.io and write IaC code to automate the entire AWS infrastructure (2 weeks). Core Web & Microservices development: write 5 backend Lambdas in Python 3.12, build the Next.js frontend, and integrate VNPay sandbox payment (2 weeks). AI RAG & event-driven integration: set up the WebSocket channel, connect EventBridge to SQS, write the background worker Lambdas, and integrate GHN sandbox shipping (2 weeks). Security, testing & go-live: fix security vulnerabilities, set up CloudWatch Alarms, and run tests (2 weeks). Technical requirements
Use Terraform to manage infrastructure consistently and make it easy to redeploy when needed. Backend written in lightweight Python 3.12 with fast startup (low cold start). Apply Zero-Trust principles: verify permissions from the Cognito token, encrypt data at rest (SSE) and in transit (HTTPS/TLS). 6. Roadmap & Milestones Weeks 1–2: Finalize the architecture and complete the base infrastructure with Terraform. Weeks 3–4: Complete the backend microservices, the shopping website, and VNPay sandbox payment. Weeks 5–6: Complete the advisory RAG chatbot, the staff handover mechanism, the SQS event queues, and GHN sandbox shipping integration. Weeks 7–8: Security testing, cost optimization, and production launch. 7. Budget Estimation Costs can be viewed on the AWS Pricing Calculator Or see the budget estimate file. Infrastructure costs (detailed estimate from the AWS spreadsheet for a scale of 1,000 users/month):
AWS Secrets Manager: USD 1.65/month (securely manages 4 secrets: Gemini Key, VNPay, GHN, Gmail SMTP; 10,000 API calls). Amazon CloudFront: USD 1.32/month (10 GB data transfer out, 50,000 HTTPS requests, and the Edge WAF filter). Amazon CloudWatch: USD 1.30/month (1 GB log data ingested, 6 metric alarms, and 1 monitoring dashboard). Amazon DynamoDB: USD 0.52/month (USD 0.29 for on-demand read/write capacity and USD 0.23 for PITR backup protecting 1 GB of data; Streams are free at USD 0). Amazon API Gateway: USD 0.23/month (50,000 REST API requests and 20,000 WebSocket messages). S3 Standard: USD 0.09/month (3 GB of image & vector storage, 1,000 PUT requests, and 15,000 GET requests). AWS Key Management Service (KMS): USD 0.03/month (10,000 symmetric requests for encrypting secret keys). AWS Lambda: USD 0.00/month (500,000 requests, 512 MB memory, fully within the 1 million requests Free Tier allowance). Amazon Cognito: USD 0.00/month (1,000 monthly active users (MAU), free within the 50,000 MAU Free Tier allowance). Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS): USD 0.00/month (15,000 standard requests, free within the 1 million requests Free Tier). Amazon EventBridge: USD 0.00/month (3,000 custom events within the Free Tier allowance). Amazon SNS: USD 0.00/month (100 free email alert requests). AWS CloudTrail: USD 0.00/month (administrative Event History for 90 days is 100% free). Total cost: USD 5.14/month, equivalent to USD 61.68/12 months (approximately ~VND 1,540,000 for a full year of operation). 8. Risk Assessment Risk matrix
Web vulnerabilities / data theft: high impact, medium probability. AI giving wrong part specifications: high impact, low probability. Cost spikes due to API spam: medium impact, low probability. Mitigation strategies
Block attacks at the edge with Edge WAF, and verify JWT tokens to prevent viewing other people’s orders (IDOR protection). Strictly constrain the AI prompt: only answer what is in the technical documents and never invent specifications. Set rate limits on API Gateway and configure AWS Budgets cost alerts. Contingency plans
When the bot cannot handle a case, it automatically escalates to a support staff member by email, together with the customer’s information. The entire infrastructure is defined in Terraform files and can be fully rebuilt in another region within 15 minutes in case of an incident. 9. Expected Results Technical improvements: Successfully build a complete Serverless e-commerce system combined with real-time AI RAG, automatically scaling with load without anyone on duty to operate servers. Practical value: Helps motorcycle parts stores reduce advisory staffing costs, lower the rate of customers buying wrong parts, and save as much budget as possible for the company/store owner.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

title: Week 8 Worklog
content:
Week 8 Objectives: Learn to evaluate the quality of RAG applications with Amazon Bedrock Evaluation. Understand how to monitor and audit AWS account activity with CloudTrail and GuardDuty. Explore Amazon Q Business for building an internal AI assistant for enterprises. Apply the Least Privilege principle with IAM Access Analyzer. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Amazon Bedrock Evaluation: evaluate the quality of RAG applications
+ 2 evaluation modes: “Retrieve only” and “Retrieve and Generate”
+ “Retrieve only” metrics: context relevance, context coverage
+ “Retrieve and Generate” metrics: correctness, completeness, helpfulness, logical coherence…
+ Process: prepare a question/answer set (JSONL) -> upload to S3 -> in the Bedrock console choose the RAG source, evaluation mode, judge model, metrics, and response-generating model -> review the result report 2/11/2026 2/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html 3 - AWS CloudTrail:
+ Records changes made through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs & APIs, and AWS internal automation
+ Event types: Management Events, Data Events, Insights Events (JSON)
+ Storage: “Event History” keeps Management Events for only 90 days; use “Trails” to deliver compressed .json.gz files to an Amazon S3 bucket for longer retention 3/11/2026 3/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/ 4 - AWS GuardDuty: intelligent threat detection using Machine Learning
+ Input data: CloudTrail Events, VPC Flow Logs, DNS Query Logs
+ Finding severity: Low, Medium, High
+ Standard format: ThreatPurpose:ResourceType/ThreatFamilyName.DetectionMechanism
+ Common findings: CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B!DNS; UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS 4/11/2026 4/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/ 5 - Amazon Q Business: generative AI assistant for enterprises based on internal data (Enterprise RAG)
+ Core components: Data Sources (40+ connectors: S3, SharePoint, Jira, Confluence, Slack…), Index (semantic indexing), Retriever, and Plugins (perform actions in third-party systems)
+ Security & permissions: integrates with AWS IAM Identity Center and uses document-level ACLs, so users only get answers from documents they are allowed to view
+ Process: create an Application -> connect IAM Identity Center -> add a Data Source & Sync it into the Index -> configure Guardrails/Admin Controls -> deploy the Web Experience for end users 5/11/2026 5/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qbusiness-ug/ 6 - IAM Access Analyzer: analyzes policies with Automated Reasoning and refines permissions toward Least Privilege
+ 4 features: External Access Analysis (finds resources shared outside the Zone of Trust, free), Unused Access Analysis (scans forgotten roles/users/access keys, paid), Policy Validation (checks syntax and 100+ security rules), Policy Generation (generates a JSON policy from real activity history)
+ Least Privilege process: enable a CloudTrail Trail (Management + Data Events) and run tests in Dev -> use Generate policy on the IAM Role to scan CloudTrail logs -> restrict Resource ARNs and check with Policy Validation -> attach the final policy to Production and enable External Access Analyzer for monitoring 6/11/2026 6/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-access-analyzer.html Week 8 Achievements: Understood the Bedrock Evaluation flow for RAG: the 2 modes, the metrics, and how to read the report. Understood which events CloudTrail records and how to keep logs beyond 90 days with Trails + S3. Understood how GuardDuty analyzes logs to detect threats, and how to read finding severity and names. Understood the Amazon Q Business architecture: Data Sources, Index, Retriever, Plugins, and access control with IAM Identity Center + ACLs. Understood the 4 features of IAM Access Analyzer and the process of generating Least Privilege policies from CloudTrail logs.

title: Week 9 Worklog
content:
Week 9 Objectives: Control the input/output safety of LLM applications with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Understand how to bring AI/ML processing to edge devices with AWS IoT Greengrass. Learn the ways to run web apps on Lambda: Function URLs and Web Adapter. Understand load balancing with ALB and running containers with Amazon ECS (Fargate/EC2). Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: safeguard layer that controls both input (prompt) and output (response) for LLM/Agent applications
+ 6 controls: Content Filters (hate speech, violence, blocks Prompt Injection/Jailbreak), Denied Topics (ban sensitive topics), Word Filters (profanity, competitor names), Sensitive Information Filters (block or mask PII/Custom Regex such as [EMAIL], [PHONE]), Contextual Grounding Checks (reduce RAG hallucination based on grounding in the source), Automated Reasoning Checks
+ Usage: integrates with Bedrock Models, Knowledge Bases, and Bedrock Agents, or can be called standalone through the ApplyGuardrail API to protect models outside Bedrock too 9/11/2026 9/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html 3 - AWS IoT Greengrass: cloud service and open-source Edge Runtime that brings AWS processing to edge devices
+ Capabilities: low-latency local data processing, offline operation when the network is lost, AI/ML inference at the edge, and remote (OTA) software/model updates for many devices
+ Architecture: package the app as Greengrass Components (Lambda functions, Docker containers, Python scripts) -> deploy from the Cloud to devices running Greengrass Core -> filter data locally and send only important data/alerts to AWS IoT Core or S3 through Stream Manager 10/11/2026 10/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/greengrass/ 4 - AWS Lambda Web Functions (Lambda Function URLs & Lambda Web Adapter): run web apps and HTTP APIs directly on Lambda
+ Lambda Function URLs: a dedicated HTTPS endpoint (https://.lambda-url..on.aws) for a Lambda function without paying for API Gateway; supports CORS, streaming responses, and 2 auth modes: AWS_IAM or NONE (public)
+ Lambda Web Adapter (Lambda Layer / Container extension): runs traditional web frameworks (Next.js, Express.js, FastAPI, Flask, Spring Boot) on Lambda as they are, without rewriting code to the Lambda event handler format 11/11/2026 11/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/urls-configuration.html 5 - Amazon ALB (Application Load Balancer): Layer 7 load balancer (HTTP/HTTPS, gRPC, WebSockets) in Elastic Load Balancing
+ Components: Listeners (ports/protocols such as 80, 443), Rules (path-based /api/*, host-based, HTTP headers, query strings), Target Groups (EC2 instances, ECS tasks/IPs, Lambda) with automatic Health Checks
+ Integration & security: free SSL/TLS certificates via AWS Certificate Manager (SSL offloading), AWS WAF integration against web attacks, Sticky Sessions and authentication via Cognito or OIDC 12/11/2026 12/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/ 6 - Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service): AWS container orchestration service
+ Components: Cluster (infrastructure group), Task Definition (JSON blueprint declaring the Docker image, CPU/RAM, ports, IAM Task Role, CloudWatch logs), Task (an instance running from a Task Definition), Service (keeps the desired number of Tasks, self-heals on failure, attaches to an ALB)
+ 2 Launch Types: AWS Fargate (serverless, no server management, billed by the vCPU and memory each Task actually uses) and Amazon EC2 (manage the EC2 cluster yourself to optimize cost for steady workloads or use GPUs) 13/11/2026 13/11/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/ Week 9 Achievements: Understood the 6 controls of Bedrock Guardrails and how to use them through the ApplyGuardrail API. Understood the Greengrass architecture: Components, Core device, Stream Manager, OTA, and offline operation. Told apart Lambda Function URLs from API Gateway and knew when to use Lambda Web Adapter. Understood ALB Listeners, Rules, Target Groups, and Health Checks, plus ACM and WAF integration. Understood ECS Clusters, Task Definitions, Tasks, and Services, and the difference between Fargate and EC2 launch types.
